The other day, I found an old shoebox tucked under my bed, its edges frayed with time. Inside were yellowed ticket stubs from a concert I’d forgotten about, a half-melted chocolate bar from a road trip in 2012, and a single, crumpled origami crane my little sister had made me when I was sick. I sat there for a while, running my fingers over the brittle paper, wondering how something so small could hold so much weight—memories, emotions, the quiet hum of a life lived.

It made me think about how we collect things: not just objects, but moments, regrets, and fleeting joys. We store them away like secrets, hoping they’ll mean something later. But sometimes, we forget to look back. We’re too busy chasing the next thing—the next job, the next relationship, the next *something*—that we miss the beauty in the already-lived.

I don’t know if I’ll ever fold another paper crane, but I’ll keep that shoebox. Maybe one day, when I’m old and my hands tremble, I’ll pull it out again and remember that life isn’t just about moving forward. It’s about the little things we carry with us, the echoes of who we were and who we’re becoming.

And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough.
